title: Best execution
text: A broker must get its customer the best result it reasonably can. Transaction cost analysis, or TCA, is how a firm checks whether it did, trade by trade, in numbers.

title: Why it matters
text: In the US, FINRA Rule 5310 requires reasonable diligence to find the best market, so the customer's price is as favorable as possible under prevailing market conditions. In the EU, MiFID II Article 27 asks for all sufficient steps to get the best possible result. That means weighing price, costs, speed, likelihood of execution and settlement, size, and the nature of the order.

title: Regular and rigorous
text: FINRA lists what diligence weighs: the character of the market, the size and type of the order, the number of markets checked, how accessible the quote is, and the order's terms. A firm that routes automatically must review execution quality at least quarterly, by security and by order type. It compares how often customers got price improvement, or a price worse than the quote, plus fill rates, speed and costs, against what other venues offered.

title: Benchmarks
text: TCA starts with a benchmark. The arrival price is the mid when the order arrived. Implementation shortfall is everything paid against it. Say you buy 1,000 shares, the arrival mid is $20.00, and your fills average $20.03. The shortfall is 3 cents a share, or $30, which is 15 basis points. It bundles the spread you crossed, your own market impact, and the drift while you waited.

title: Spread capture and markouts
text: For a market maker, two numbers matter. Spread capture compares the fill with the mid just before it. A passive buy at $19.99, with the mid at $20.00, captures one cent. The markout compares the same fill with the mid a little later. If the mid is $19.97 one second on, the markout is minus two cents. The three cent gap is adverse selection: the trade told you the price was about to move.

title: In the lab
text: The lab's research tools compute exactly these. For each fill, spread capture uses the last mid strictly before the fill, because the exchange stamps a fill and the market data it causes with the same time. Markouts follow at 1 millisecond, 10 milliseconds, 100 milliseconds and 1 second. The summary gives cents per share and basis points, so changes to the strategy can be compared.

title: Takeaway
text: So what do pros do? They choose the benchmark before they trade, not after. They measure by venue, order type and size, not as one average. They separate spread paid from adverse selection. And they keep the evidence, because a review is only as good as its data. This is education, not legal advice.
